topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Applicability
question: Under Michigan's Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92, MCL 565.951-565.966), which category of real estate transfer is generally SUBJECT to the act's seller disclosure requirements?
choice_a: A commercial office building sale
choice_b: A transfer of unimproved agricultural land with no dwelling
choice_c: A sale of a residential dwelling containing between 1 and 4 units
choice_d: A transfer of a 6-unit apartment building
explanation: MCL 565.952 applies the Act's disclosure requirements to transfers of any interest in real estate consisting of not less than 1 or more than 4 residential dwelling units, by sale, exchange, installment land contract, lease with an option to purchase, or similar transfer, including a transfer of stock or an interest in a residential cooperative.
source_note: MCL 565.952, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Exemptions (family transfers)
question: Which of the following transfers is EXEMPT from the Seller Disclosure Act's disclosure requirements under MCL 565.953?
choice_a: A sale of a single-family home to an unrelated buyer through a licensed broker
choice_b: An installment land contract sale to a first-time homebuyer
choice_c: A lease with an option to purchase entered into with an unrelated tenant
choice_d: A transfer of the property from a seller to her adult daughter
explanation: MCL 565.953(f) exempts transfers made to a spouse, parent, grandparent, child, or grandchild from the Act's disclosure requirements.
source_note: MCL 565.953(f), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Exemptions (court-ordered/foreclosure transfers)
question: A property is transferred through a court-ordered probate estate administration sale. Under MCL 565.953, how does the Seller Disclosure Act treat this transfer?
choice_a: The transfer is exempt from the seller disclosure requirements because it occurs pursuant to a court order
choice_b: The estate's personal representative must still complete and deliver the standard disclosure form
choice_c: The exemption applies only if the heirs also sign a waiver
choice_d: The transfer is exempt only if the property was inhabited within the last year
explanation: MCL 565.953(a) exempts transfers pursuant to court order -- including transfers ordered by a probate court in administration of an estate, writ-of-execution transfers, foreclosure sales, bankruptcy trustee transfers, eminent domain transfers, and transfers by decree for specific performance -- from the Act's disclosure requirements.
source_note: MCL 565.953(a), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Exemptions (new construction)
question: A Michigan-licensed builder sells a newly constructed home that has never been occupied. Under MCL 565.953(i), how does this affect the seller disclosure requirement?
choice_a: The builder must still complete the full statutory disclosure form before closing
choice_b: The transfer is exempt from the Act's disclosure requirements because it is uninhabited new construction sold by a licensee under Article 24 of the Occupational Code
choice_c: The exemption applies only to condominiums, not single-family homes
choice_d: The buyer may waive the exemption and demand disclosure
explanation: MCL 565.953(i) exempts transfers of newly constructed residential property that has not been inhabited, made by a person licensed under Article 24 of 1980 PA 299 (residential builders), from the Act's disclosure requirements.
source_note: MCL 565.953(i), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Timing of delivery (sale)
question: In a standard residential sale subject to the Seller Disclosure Act, when must the seller deliver the written disclosure statement to the prospective buyer?
choice_a: Within 10 days after the purchase agreement is signed
choice_b: At the closing table, along with the deed
choice_c: Before the seller executes a binding purchase agreement with the prospective buyer
choice_d: Only if the buyer specifically requests it in writing
explanation: MCL 565.954(1)(a) requires that in the case of a sale, the disclosure statement be delivered to the prospective transferee before the transferor executes a binding purchase agreement.
source_note: MCL 565.954(1)(a), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Timing of delivery (installment contract)
question: A seller plans to convey Michigan residential property via an installment land contract without first signing a separate purchase agreement. Under MCL 565.954(1)(b), when must the disclosure statement be delivered?
choice_a: Within 72 hours after the contract is recorded
choice_b: Any time before the final installment payment is made
choice_c: Disclosure is not required for installment land contracts
choice_d: Before the seller executes the installment sales contract with the prospective buyer
explanation: MCL 565.954(1)(b) requires delivery before the transferor executes the installment sales contract in cases where no separate binding purchase agreement was executed first; the same before-execution timing applies to a lease with an option to purchase or a ground lease coupled with tenant improvements.
source_note: MCL 565.954(1)(b), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Buyer termination right (in-person delivery)
question: A Michigan seller delivers the disclosure statement to the buyer in person, but only after the buyer already signed a binding purchase agreement. Under MCL 565.954(3)(a), how long does the buyer have to terminate the agreement by delivering written notice?
choice_a: Not later than 72 hours after delivery of the disclosure statement
choice_b: Not later than 24 hours after delivery of the disclosure statement
choice_c: Not later than 10 business days after delivery of the disclosure statement
choice_d: The buyer has no termination right once the purchase agreement is signed
explanation: MCL 565.954(3)(a) gives the buyer until not later than 72 hours after delivery of the disclosure statement to terminate, if the statement (or an amendment to it) was delivered to the buyer in person after the binding purchase agreement was already executed.
source_note: MCL 565.954(3)(a), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Buyer termination right (registered mail)
question: If a late-delivered Michigan seller disclosure statement is sent to the buyer by registered mail rather than delivered in person, how long does the buyer have to deliver written notice of termination under MCL 565.954(3)(b)?
choice_a: Not later than 72 hours after delivery of the disclosure statement
choice_b: Not later than 120 hours after delivery of the disclosure statement
choice_c: Not later than 30 days after delivery of the disclosure statement
choice_d: Not later than 48 hours after the postmark date
explanation: MCL 565.954(3)(b) extends the termination window to not later than 120 hours after delivery when the disclosure statement is delivered to the prospective transferee by registered mail, accounting for mailing time (versus 72 hours for in-person delivery).
source_note: MCL 565.954(3)(b), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Termination right expires on transfer
question: A Michigan buyer received a late disclosure statement and had a right to terminate the purchase agreement, but the deed transferring the property was recorded before the buyer sent a termination notice. Under MCL 565.954(4), what is the effect?
choice_a: The buyer may still terminate and unwind the closed transaction within 72 hours of recording
choice_b: The termination right survives transfer indefinitely if the seller acted in bad faith
choice_c: The buyer's right to terminate the purchase agreement has expired because the property was already transferred by deed
choice_d: The termination right converts automatically into a claim for rescission of the deed
explanation: MCL 565.954(4) provides that a transferee's right to terminate the purchase agreement expires upon the transfer of the subject property by deed or installment sales contract.
source_note: MCL 565.954(4), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Liability safe harbor (no personal knowledge, ordinary care)
question: A Michigan seller relayed information from a public agency record in the disclosure statement, exercising ordinary care, but the information turned out to be inaccurate through no fault of the seller. Under MCL 565.955(1), is the seller liable?
choice_a: Yes, sellers are strictly liable for any inaccuracy in the disclosure statement regardless of source
choice_b: No, but only if the buyer signed a separate liability waiver
choice_c: Yes, unless the seller obtained title insurance covering disclosure errors
choice_d: No, the seller is not liable because the inaccuracy was not within the seller's personal knowledge, was based on information from a public agency, and ordinary care was exercised in transmitting it
explanation: MCL 565.955(1) shields a transferor from liability for an error, inaccuracy, or omission that was not within the transferor's personal knowledge or was based entirely on information from a public agency (or a qualifying expert under subsection 3), provided ordinary care was exercised in transmitting it. It is also not a violation to fail to disclose information obtainable only through inspection of inaccessible areas or requiring expertise beyond the seller's knowledge.
source_note: MCL 565.955(1), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Expert report reliance
question: A Michigan seller obtains a written report from a licensed professional engineer at the buyer's request regarding structural conditions, and includes it to satisfy disclosure obligations. Under MCL 565.955(3), what is the effect?
choice_a: Delivering the qualifying expert's report is sufficient compliance for the liability exemption, unless the seller knows of a defect that contradicts the report
choice_b: The seller remains fully liable for anything the engineer's report gets wrong
choice_c: Expert reports can never be used to satisfy disclosure requirements, only the statutory form can
choice_d: The engineer, not the seller, becomes liable for all disclosures on the form going forward
explanation: MCL 565.955(3) allows delivery of a report from a licensed professional engineer, professional surveyor, geologist, structural pest control operator, contractor, or other qualifying expert (provided at the buyer's request) to serve as sufficient compliance for the liability exemption, unless the seller has knowledge of a defect or condition that contradicts the report.
source_note: MCL 565.955(3), Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Subsequent inaccuracy not a violation
question: A Michigan seller accurately disclosed that the roof had no known leaks. Two weeks after delivering the disclosure statement (before closing), a storm caused a new leak. Under MCL 565.956, is this a violation of the Seller Disclosure Act?
choice_a: Yes, the seller must have disclosed the possibility of future storm damage
choice_b: No, because the resulting inaccuracy occurred as a result of an action or occurrence after the delivery of the required disclosures
choice_c: Yes, unless the seller immediately rescinds the sale
choice_d: No, but only if the buyer had already waived inspection rights
explanation: MCL 565.956 provides that if disclosed information becomes inaccurate as a result of any action, occurrence, or agreement after delivery of the required disclosures, the resulting inaccuracy does not constitute a violation of the Act.
source_note: MCL 565.956, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Statutory form environmental problems item
question: The statutory disclosure form's "Environmental Problems" item (MCL 565.957) specifically asks the seller to disclose awareness of which of the following categories of substances or conditions?
choice_a: Only lead-based paint, since that is the sole federally mandated item
choice_b: Only substances listed on the EPA's Superfund National Priorities List
choice_c: Asbestos, radon gas, formaldehyde, lead-based paint, fuel or chemical storage tanks, and contaminated soil
choice_d: Mold and pest infestation only
explanation: The statutory form asks whether the seller is aware of any substances, materials, or products that may be an environmental hazard, "such as, but not limited to, asbestos, radon gas, formaldehyde, lead-based paint, fuel or chemical storage tanks and contaminated soil on the property."
source_note: MCL 565.957, statutory disclosure form, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Broker liability limitation on statutory form
question: The statutory Michigan Seller's Disclosure Statement form includes language addressing the real estate broker's liability for representations on the form. What does it say?
choice_a: The listing broker is jointly and severally liable with the seller for every item on the form
choice_b: The broker must co-sign the disclosure statement to be valid
choice_c: The broker is presumed to have independently verified every item on the form
choice_d: In no event shall the parties hold the broker liable for any representations not directly made by the broker or the broker's agent
explanation: The statutory form states that the disclosures are "representations made solely by the seller and are not the representations of the seller's agent(s)" and that "[i]n no event shall the parties hold the broker liable for any representations not directly made by the broker or broker's agent."
source_note: MCL 565.957, statutory disclosure form, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Additional local disclosures permitted
question: May a Michigan city, township, or county impose disclosure obligations beyond those required by the state Seller Disclosure Act's statutory form?
choice_a: Yes, MCL 565.959 allows a city, township, or county to require additional disclosures, potentially on a different disclosure form, for transactions subject to the Act
choice_b: No, the state statutory form fully preempts any local disclosure requirements
choice_c: Only counties, not cities or townships, may add disclosure requirements
choice_d: Additional local disclosures are permitted only for commercial property transactions
explanation: MCL 565.959 expressly allows a city, township, or county to require disclosures in addition to those required by section 7, including on a different disclosure form, in connection with transactions subject to the Act.
source_note: MCL 565.959, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Good faith standard
question: The Seller Disclosure Act requires every disclosure to be made in "good faith." How does MCL 565.960 define good faith for purposes of the Act?
choice_a: Compliance with all applicable local building codes
choice_b: Honesty in fact in the conduct of the transaction
choice_c: Reliance exclusively on a licensed home inspector's report
choice_d: Disclosure of only those defects a reasonable buyer would discover on a walk-through
explanation: MCL 565.960 defines "good faith," for purposes of the Act, as "honesty in fact in the conduct of the transaction."
source_note: MCL 565.960, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Amendment subject to timing rules
question: A Michigan seller wants to amend a previously delivered disclosure statement in writing after discovering a new defect. Under MCL 565.962, how does this amendment interact with the rest of the Act?
choice_a: Amendments are prohibited once the original disclosure statement has been delivered
choice_b: An amendment automatically voids the original purchase agreement
choice_c: The amendment is permitted but remains subject to section 4's delivery timing rules, which can trigger the buyer's termination right if delivered after a binding purchase agreement is signed
choice_d: Amendments need only be delivered orally to be effective
explanation: MCL 565.962 allows a transferor to amend a disclosure made under the Act in writing, but expressly states the amendment "is subject to section 4," meaning the same delivery-timing and buyer termination-right rules under MCL 565.954 apply to the amendment.
source_note: MCL 565.962, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Transfer not invalidated by noncompliance
question: A Michigan seller completely failed to deliver any disclosure statement before closing, and the property has already transferred by deed. Under MCL 565.964, what happens to the transfer itself?
choice_a: The transfer is automatically void and title reverts to the seller
choice_b: The buyer may force the seller to repurchase the property at the original price
choice_c: The county register of deeds must refuse to record the transfer
choice_d: The transfer is not invalidated solely because of the failure to comply with the Act; the buyer's principal remedy was the pre-closing right to terminate
explanation: MCL 565.964 provides that a transfer subject to the Act "shall not be invalidated solely because of the failure of any person to comply with a provision of this act" -- the Act's enforcement mechanism is primarily the buyer's pre-closing termination right under section 4 (MCL 565.954), not invalidation of a completed transfer.
source_note: MCL 565.964, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Seller Disclosure Act – Agent liability limitation
question: Under MCL 565.965, when is a real estate agent representing the seller liable for the seller's violation of the Seller Disclosure Act?
choice_a: An agent is not liable for the transferor's violation of the Act unless the agent knowingly acts in concert with the transferor to violate the Act
choice_b: The agent is automatically liable for any inaccuracy in the seller's disclosure statement
choice_c: The agent is liable only if the agent personally drafted the disclosure statement
choice_d: Agent liability under the Act was eliminated entirely by a 2005 amendment
explanation: MCL 565.965 provides that an agent of a transferor is not liable for a violation of the Act by the transferor unless the agent knowingly acts in concert with the transferor to violate the Act.
source_note: MCL 565.965, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Federal lead-based paint disclosure
question: A Michigan broker is listing a home built in 1965. Under the federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act and its implementing regulations, what disclosure obligation applies to this pre-1978 housing sale, independent of Michigan's Seller Disclosure Act?
choice_a: No federal lead disclosure applies because the home is not a rental property
choice_b: The seller must disclose known lead-based paint hazards, provide any available reports, give the buyer the EPA lead hazard information pamphlet, and afford the buyer a 10-day opportunity for a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment before becoming obligated under the contract
choice_c: Federal law requires the seller to fully remediate any lead-based paint before closing
choice_d: Lead-based paint disclosure is required only for homes built before 1950
explanation: Federal law (42 U.S.C. 4852d and implementing regulations at 24 CFR Part 35 / 40 CFR Part 745) requires sellers of housing built before 1978 to disclose known lead-based paint hazards, provide available reports, distribute the EPA pamphlet, and give buyers a 10-day inspection opportunity -- separate from and in addition to any state seller disclosure form requirements.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (42 U.S.C. 4852d; 24 CFR Part 35; 40 CFR Part 745)

topic: Material fact / material defect doctrine
question: Under general national real estate agency and disclosure principles that apply regardless of a specific state disclosure statute, how is a "material defect" typically distinguished from a minor, immaterial condition?
choice_a: A material defect is any condition costing more than $500 to repair, as a bright-line rule used nationwide
choice_b: Only defects visible to the naked eye during a walkthrough are ever considered material
choice_c: A material defect is a condition that would significantly affect the value or desirability of the property, or that a reasonable buyer would want to know about before deciding to purchase or how much to offer
choice_d: Material defects apply only to structural elements, never to environmental or legal conditions
explanation: As a general national principle independent of any single state statute, a material fact or material defect is one that would significantly affect a reasonable buyer's decision to purchase or the price offered -- as opposed to trivial or purely cosmetic conditions, which are not considered material regardless of jurisdiction.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles

topic: Environmental contamination disclosure beyond the checkbox list
question: A Michigan seller has actual knowledge that a previous underground heating-oil storage tank leaked and contaminated soil on the property, but this fact is not itemized in exactly those words on the statutory disclosure form. Under general disclosure principles reinforcing Michigan's statutory scheme, must the seller still disclose it?
choice_a: No -- sellers are only ever required to disclose items that appear as a specific checkbox on the statutory form
choice_b: No -- environmental contamination is exclusively the buyer's responsibility to discover through due diligence
choice_c: Yes, but only if the seller is a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Yes -- known material facts and defects generally must be disclosed even beyond the specific items enumerated on a standard form, and MCL 565.961 confirms the Act does not limit other disclosure obligations arising from fraud, misrepresentation, or deceit law
explanation: MCL 565.961 states that the Act's specified disclosure items do not limit or abridge any other disclosure obligation created by law regarding fraud, misrepresentation, or deceit -- and the statutory form's "Environmental Problems" and "underground storage tanks" items, together with general material-fact doctrine, support disclosing known contamination such as a leaking underground storage tank.
source_note: MCL 565.961, Seller Disclosure Act (1993 PA 92); hedge: standard national real estate principles for the underlying material-fact doctrine

topic: Right to Farm Act voluntary farm-proximity disclosure
question: A Michigan property lies within one mile of an active farm operation. Under MCL 286.473c of the Michigan Right to Farm Act, what disclosure practice is authorized in connection with the sale of that property?
choice_a: A seller may voluntarily provide the buyer a statement informing them the property lies within one mile of a farm or farm operation, and that generally accepted agricultural practices may generate usual noise, dust, and odors protected under the Right to Farm Act
choice_b: Sellers are legally required to obtain a written waiver from every neighboring farm operator before closing
choice_c: Properties within one mile of a farm operation cannot legally be sold as residential property
choice_d: The buyer must personally inspect the farm operation and sign an acknowledgment at the county register of deeds
explanation: MCL 286.473c authorizes (but does not mandate) a seller of property within one mile of a farm or farm operation to voluntarily provide the buyer a statement noting the proximity and that generally accepted agricultural and management practices generating usual noise, dust, and odors are protected from nuisance claims under the Michigan Right to Farm Act -- consistent with the statutory Seller's Disclosure Statement's own farm-proximity question.
source_note: MCL 286.473c, Michigan Right to Farm Act (1981 PA 93), verified via legislature.mi.gov

topic: Private road disclosure (Land Division Act)
question: A Michigan parcel abuts a road that has never been accepted as a public road by the county road commission. Under MCL 560.261 of the Land Division Act, what must the seller do before conveying the lot?
choice_a: Pave the private road to county standards before any sale can close
choice_b: Inform the purchaser in writing, on a separate instrument attached to the conveying instrument, that the road is private and not required to be maintained by the county road commissioners
choice_c: Obtain a variance from the county road commission before listing the property
choice_d: Nothing -- private road status need not be disclosed under Michigan law
explanation: MCL 560.261 requires that before selling a platted lot or unplatted parcel abutting a road not accepted as public, the seller must inform the purchaser in writing, on a separate instrument attached to the instrument conveying the interest, that the road is private and not required to be maintained by the board of county road commissioners; a sale made in violation of this section is voidable at the purchaser's option.
source_note: MCL 560.261, Land Division Act (1967 PA 288), verified via legislature.mi.gov
